summary: Changes and clarifies the semantics of the Type of Service octet in the IP header, which lets a sender hint how a packet should be treated. It was replaced by RFC 2474.

eli5.summary: Some packages need to arrive fast, others cheaply. A small label in the packet header says which kind it is, and this document explains how to read it.

subtitle: How to request network paths optimized for delay, throughput, reliability, or cost

tldr.problem: Internet paths vary in reliability, latency, throughput, and cost. Applications need a way to hint which matters most, and routers need to know how to handle those hints.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1349 defines a 4-bit TOS field in the IP header that can hold one of five values: minimize delay (1000), maximize throughput (0100), maximize reliability (0010), minimize cost (0001), or normal service (0000). Routers and hosts use this field to select paths with matching characteristics.
tldr.outcome: TOS support required significant router deployment and remained limited. RFC 2474 later redefined TOS as DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) with different semantics for modern QoS mechanisms.

today: RFC 2474 redefined the Type of Service octet as the Differentiated Services (DiffServ) field in December 1998. The TOS concept largely faded from deployment due to limited router support and management complexity. Modern networks use DSCP and Quality of Service mechanisms like IntServ and DiffServ instead.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IP header contains a Type of Service octet with three fields: a 3-bit PRECEDENCE field, a 4-bit TOS field (changed from 3 bits in RFC 791), and a 1-bit MBZ (must-be-zero) field. RFC 1349 specifies how the TOS field should be interpreted and used.

TOS is an advisory mechanism allowing upper-layer protocols to hint to the IP layer about path optimization preferences. The Internet host specification now mandates that hosts use the TOS facility. Routing protocols like OSPF and Integrated IS-IS can compute separate routes for different TOS values, making the mechanism practical.
sections.eli5: Your package can ask to be sent fast, cheap, reliably, or at high speed. Networks and routers read the label and do their best.

sections.title: TOS Field Values and Philosophy
sections.content:
RFC 1349 changes the TOS field from a set of independent bits to a single enumerated value (4 bits wide). The five defined values are:

  • 1000 (8): minimize delay
  • 0100 (4): maximize throughput
  • 0010 (2): maximize reliability
  • 0001 (1): minimize monetary cost
  • 0000 (0): normal service (default)

A fundamental principle: a host should never be penalized for using the TOS facility. If a network cannot provide the requested TOS, it delivers the packet anyway rather than discarding it. The words 'minimize' and 'maximize' are important: a request for low delay does not guarantee low delay, only that the network will choose the lowest-delay path available.
sections.eli5: You can ask for speed, throughput, reliability, or low cost. The network tries its best, but never punishes you for asking.

sections.title: How Hosts and Applications Use TOS
sections.content:
The ICMP protocol must always send error messages with the default TOS (0000). ICMP request messages (echo, router discovery) can use any TOS value. ICMP reply messages use the same TOS as the corresponding request.

Transport protocols like TCP use TOS requested by the application. Both ends of a connection can use different TOS values; for example, bulk data might request maximized throughput while acknowledgements request minimized delay. TCP segments containing only control information use the same TOS as data segments to avoid corrupting round-trip time estimates.

Applications are responsible for choosing appropriate TOS values. RFC 1060 (Assigned Numbers) lists TOS values for common applications: TELNET and FTP control use minimize-delay, FTP data uses maximize-throughput, SMTP command phase uses minimize-delay and data phase uses maximize-throughput.
sections.eli5: The program decides what matters (speed, volume, or cost), tells the network, and the network routes accordingly.

sections.title: Routing with TOS Support
sections.content:
RFC 1349 defines weak TOS routing: when forwarding, a router first looks for a route matching both the destination and the requested TOS. If not found, the router uses the default TOS (0000) route if available. If neither exists, the destination is unreachable.

For ICMP Redirects, routers use code 3 (for TOS-specific redirects) and code 1 (for non-TOS redirects). Hosts maintain two types of route cache entries: TOS-specific routes {destination, TOS, router} and general routes {destination, *, router}. When creating a general route, hosts must flush any TOS-specific routes to the same destination to maintain correctness.

Hosts treat ICMP Redirects as hints, not proof, that a destination is unreachable. Code 11 and code 12 unreachable messages indicate the destination is unreachable for the requested TOS but reachable with a different TOS.
sections.eli5: The router remembers 'to reach this place with low delay, use this path' and 'to reach this place normally, use that path'. If the requested path doesn't exist, it tries the normal one.

sections.title: Limitations and Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
TOS is an advisory, not a guarantee. It works only in routing domains where network managers configure TOS-aware routers and policies. Many networks don't use TOS because their paths are homogeneous; others lack the configuration expertise. Long appendices in the RFC explain the design rationale and limitations in detail.

Two key limitations: TOS cannot guarantee specific service levels (an application requesting maximize-throughput cannot specify a required minimum bandwidth), and routing is not optimal for all TOS values (computing a path that maximizes reliability requires special algorithms, not standard metric summation).

The RFC assumes network managers 'do the right thing.' A misconfigured manager can violate the principle that using TOS should not penalize hosts. RFC 1349 updates several other RFCs (RFC 791, 792, 1060, 1122, 1123, 1195, 1247, 1248) to align their TOS handling.
sections.eli5: TOS works well only if everyone believes in it and sets it up carefully. There is no magic: if the network has only one path, TOS doesn't help.
